analysis.one_liner: Expands background checks to most private gun sales, caps handgun purchases, funds red-flag laws, and closes domestic-violence loopholes.
analysis.headline: The Senate referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and it never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require that nearly all private gun sales go through a licensed dealer who runs a background check, limit most people to one handgun purchase per 30 days, and create a national framework for 'red flag' orders letting courts temporarily bar dangerous individuals from having guns. It also closes gaps that let dating partners and convicted stalkers keep firearms, requires reporting lost or stolen guns within 48 hours, and makes it a crime to recklessly leave a loaded, unsecured gun where a child can reach it. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never moved further.
analysis.who_benefits: Survivors of domestic violence, who would no longer face abusers they dated; families and communities at risk of gun suicide or mass violence, who gain the protection-order tool; police, who gain training grants and a requirement that lost and stolen guns be reported, making gun trafficking easier to trace.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Domestic violence survivors and communities at risk

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits private firearm transfers unless a licensed dealer first conducts a background check, closing the sales channel that does not require any check, while exempting transfers between close family, gifts, hunting, range use, and transfers in the owner's presence.

Establishes a federal framework and grant program for extreme risk protection orders ('red flag' laws), under which a court finding by a preponderance of evidence that a person is dangerous can bar gun possession, with written notice, a hearing within 30 days, and ex parte orders capped at 30 days.

Expands the federal domestic-violence firearm ban to cover dating partners and makes misdemeanor stalking convictions a bar to gun possession, both with counsel and jury-trial protections for the accused.

Requires notification of law enforcement within 48 hours when a firearm is lost or stolen (a $250 civil penalty for failure), and makes it a crime, punishable by up to one year in prison, to recklessly leave a loaded and unsecured firearm where it endangers a person under 14.

Limits non-dealers to purchasing one handgun in any 30-day period, aimed at trafficking purchases, with exceptions including law enforcement, licensed security companies, and people who pass an enhanced background check.

analysis.who_pays: Private gun owners and sellers bear new compliance costs: paying a dealer to facilitate each transfer, the one-handgun-per-month limit, reporting obligations, and new penalties. Federal taxpayers fund the grant program, and courts and police absorb the work of running protection-order hearings and storing removed firearms.

drawbacks.text: The bill bars any regulation capping the fee a licensed dealer may charge to facilitate a private-sale background check, leaving the cost of compliance entirely to whatever dealers choose to charge.

Ex parte red-flag orders can direct the surrender or removal of firearms before the named person has been heard, with only a hearing within 30 days to follow; orders remain in effect until a court terminates them, which raises civil-liberties concerns for gun owners.

The one-handgun-per-30-days limit applies broadly to non-dealers and depends on states issuing enhanced-check certificates for exceptions, adding delays for collectors and competitive shooters even though most gun crimes involve few guns.
Background checks do not stop guns that are already in circulation from being stolen or resold underground, and the bill's authorization of grant funding is not an actual appropriation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The loopholes it closes are real ones: people with domestic-violence histories involving dating partners, convicted stalkers, and buyers who avoid checks through private sales can currently obtain guns. The compliance costs on ordinary owners are modest but unpriced, since the bill leaves dealer facilitation fees uncapped, and the red-flag framework includes only the minimum due-process floor for states. On balance the protections would likely outweigh the burdens, but the design leaves cost and civil-liberties questions open that Congress never took up.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and sent to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Kaine introduced the bill in the Senate on July 22, 2020, joined by Sen. Mark Warner as its sole cosponsor.
On the day of introduction, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on the Judiciary.
No hearing, committee markup, floor debate, or vote on the bill is recorded in its action history; the referral was the last action before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, private sellers who avoid background checks kept selling without them, and no dealer facilitation market, purchase limits, or red-flag requirements took effect. Gun owners subject to its proposed restrictions kept the status quo, while people exposed to the risks the bill targeted — dating-partner abusers, stalkers, and untraceable trafficking purchases — faced no new federal limits.

industries.note: The bill makes the dealer the required middleman for nearly every private gun sale and explicitly bars the Attorney General from capping the fee a dealer may charge for it. Dealers gain a paid facilitation role on every transfer, riding on a public-safety mandate rather than against it.

industries.industry: Unlicensed private sellers and secondary-market gun sales
industries.note: Private sales without any background check would become unlawful, closing the channel most often used for untraceable gun transfers. Sellers operating outside the licensed system would lose that market.

The one-handgun-per-30-days purchase limit could trim volume from multi-gun buyers, but most retail sales go through licensed dealers and are unaffected. The bill imposes recordkeeping and notice duties on licensees without capping the fees they can charge.
